reason: The decision guide quote says to consider AWS Site-to-Site VPN to securely connect an entire on-premises network to your VPCs.
The quote says Amazon provides an ASN for the virtual gateway if you do not choose one, and after June 30th 2018 that ASN is 64512.
The quote defines a VPN connection in the guide as the connection between your VPC and your on-premises network and says Site-to-Site VPN supports IPsec VPN connections.
Under the heading 'Which Diffie-Hellman groups do you support?' the two value lines give Phase 1 groups 2, 14-24 and Phase 2 groups 2, 5, 14-24.
The quote states the default DPD timeout action (IKE session stopped, tunnel down, routes removed) and the restart or no-action alternatives.
The quote explains the DPD timeout in seconds, says you can specify 30 or higher, and gives Default: 40.
The quote lists BGP peering, binding tunnels to logical interfaces and IPsec Dead Peer Detection as musts for dynamically routed devices.
The quote states ECMP on a transit gateway aggregates tunnels, needs dynamic routing, and is not supported with static routing.
The quote says one tunnel is selected on a virtual private gateway, ECMP is supported on a transit gateway and not on a virtual private gateway.
Under the heading 'How tunnel endpoint lifecycle control works' the quotes give the AWS Health notifications and the automatic replacement soon after the Maintenance auto applied after date.

The quote supports control over the schedule of replacements, but the note right after it says AWS might apply critical updates immediately even with the feature enabled; the claim drops this exception.
The quote says endpoints are replaced on AWS tunnel updates or your modifications and that connectivity might be interrupted during replacement.
The quote states updates go to one tunnel at a time, redundancy may be briefly lost, and both tunnels should be configured for high availability.
The quote gives the create-new, repoint, delete-old steps and the new tunnel IP addresses because of separate IP ranges.
Under the heading on creating an Accelerated Site-to-Site VPN, the quote says to set Enable Acceleration to true when creating the connection.
The quote states NAT-T is required and enabled by default for Accelerated Site-to-Site VPN connections.
The quote says it can only be created through Site-to-Site VPN and not through the Global Accelerator console or API.
The quote says it is not available over public Direct Connect VIFs and in most cases gives no acceleration benefit there.
The quote begins 'Other that that' and supports the same protocols, bandwidth, options and auth types, but the NAT-T exception the claim names stands only in the preceding sentence, not in the quote.
The quote says only Transit Gateway supports it, a Transit Gateway is specified at creation, and the AWS-side endpoint is created on it.
Under the heading asking whether an Accelerated connection offers two tunnels, the quote says each VPN connection offers two tunnels for high availability.
The FAQ quote says the VPN connection advertises a maximum of 1,000 routes to the customer gateway device (note: the quotas page table gives 5,000 for transit gateway; a separate fact).
The quote states the BGP session resets if you advertise more than the maximum for the gateway type.
The quote says by default the CGW must initiate IKE and the AWS endpoints can initiate when the options are enabled.
The quote states transit gateway VPNs carry IPv4 or IPv6 chosen at creation, via Inside IP Version, with tunnel endpoint and CGW addresses IPv4 only.
The quote states the interruption of up to several minutes and that logging can be enabled one tunnel at a time with only that tunnel impacted.
The quote states each private IP VPN connection supports 1.25Gbps and 5Gbps like regular connections and ECMP increases effective bandwidth.
The quote recommends BGP-capable devices when available for robust liveness detection that assists failover to the second tunnel.
The quote states private IP VPN connections support 1500 bytes of MTU.
The quote states private IP VPN deploys to a Transit Gateway with private IPs and works over a Direct Connect transit VIF.
The quote gives a maximum of 100 routes on a virtual private gateway and 1000 on a Transit Gateway from the customer gateway device.
The quote states a static-route VPN connection cannot have more than 100 static routes.
Under the heading on the virtual private gateway aggregate throughput limit, the quote says to use Transit Gateway for multiple VPCs and higher throughput limits.
The quote lists the same throughput factors as the claim.
The quote states two tunnels per connection, each up to 140,000 packets per second.
The quote states two tunnels per connection, each up to 1.25 Gbps, with aggregated limits on a virtual private gateway.
The quote states the aggregate limit of up to 1.25 Gbps from AWS to on-premises for multiple VPNs on one virtual private gateway and the Direct Connect port bound.
The quote says the Amazon side ASN cannot be modified after creation and you recreate the virtual gateway with the desired ASN.
The quote supports the reason (no ownership validation, BGP spoofing), but nearby answers make an exception for the region's legacy public ASN, which the claim's 'limited to private ASNs' drops.
Under 'What ASN can I choose?' in the virtual private gateway section, the quote gives any private ASN, 16-bit 64512 to 65534 and 32-bit 4200000000 to 4294967294.
The whitepaper quote states both the forward to on-premises DNS and the response to queries forwarded from on-premises.
The quote states AES128 or AES256, Diffie-Hellman groups with Perfect Forward Secrecy, and SHA1 or SHA2 authentication per tunnel.
The quote supports IPv4 by default and IPv6 on a new connection, but 'on a transit gateway' (claim and scope) stands only in the preceding sentence, not in the quote.
The quote states IPv6 is not supported on a virtual private gateway and outer-tunnel IPv6 only on Transit Gateway and Cloud WAN.
The two quotes state one connection cannot carry both IPv4 and IPv6 and an existing IPv4 connection cannot be modified to IPv6.
The quote supports that both count toward the per-Region connections quota, but the qualifier 'adjustable: true' is not stated in the quote.
Table row 'Maximum bandwidth per VPN Concentrator VPN tunnel | Up to 100 Mbps | No' under Name | Default | Adjustable.
The table row gives up to 5 Gbps, not adjustable; the What's New quote gives the previous 1.25 Gbps limit.
Table row 'Maximum bandwidth per standard VPN tunnel | Up to 1.25 Gbps | No'.
The quote gives 5,000 routes transit gateway to customer gateway and 1,000 customer gateway to transit gateway per site.
The quote gives ECMP for more than 5 Gbps per tunnel and the 20 Gbps example with two connections and four tunnels.
The quote states the same throughput, MTU and route limits and no performance difference.
The quote states MTU 1446 bytes and MSS 1406 bytes.
Table row gives up to 10,000 PPS per VPN Concentrator tunnel, not adjustable.
Table row gives up to 400,000 PPS per large bandwidth tunnel, not adjustable.
Table row gives up to 140,000 PPS per standard tunnel, not adjustable.
The quote gives 5000 outbound and 1000 inbound for private IP VPN versus 200 and 100 for Direct Connect alone.
Table row gives 1,000 dynamic routes from the customer gateway to a transit gateway VPN, not adjustable.
Table row gives 100 dynamic routes from the customer gateway to a virtual private gateway VPN, not adjustable.
Table row gives 5,000 routes from a transit gateway VPN to the customer gateway, not adjustable (the FAQ states 1,000 generally; worth a conflict check).
Table row gives 1,000 routes from a virtual private gateway VPN to the customer gateway, not adjustable.
Table row gives 100 static routes to a virtual private gateway VPN, not adjustable.
The quote states the local route is most preferred over overlapping propagated VPN or Direct Connect routes even when they are more specific.
The quote lists IPsec, IKE, DPD and BGP details and says the logs can be published to CloudWatch Logs.
The quote supports longest prefix match, but the next bullet gives an exception (the local route wins even over more specific propagated routes), which the unqualified claim drops.
The table row defines TunnelDataIn as bytes received on the AWS side from the customer gateway, counted after decryption.
The table row defines TunnelDataOut as bytes sent from the AWS side to the customer gateway, counted before encryption.
The table row gives the static and BGP meanings of 0 and 1 and that values between 0 and 1 mean at least one tunnel is not UP.

The quote states the IDr requirement, but it sits in the 'Rules and limitations' list for IKE initiation options (AWS-side initiation); the claim states it with no such scope, and the quote alone does not settle whether it applies generally.
The quote says to disable NAT-T on the device; otherwise AWS tries UDP 4500 and the tunnel does not establish if the port is closed.
The table row gives the use case and the two limitations named in the claim.
The quote states the service is route-based and a policy-based solution must be limited to a single SA.
The quote states the per connection-hour charge for a 5Gbps connection plus standard data transfer charges.
The quotes give normal connection pricing plus two Global Accelerators and DT-Premium, and no Global Accelerator charges for non-accelerated VPNs.
The quote states the Concentrator-hour charge and the per connection-hour charge for connections via the concentrator.
The quote supports data transfer out charges explained on the EC2 on-demand pricing page, but the scope 'per gigabyte' is not stated in the quote.
The quote states no extra Site-to-Site VPN charge for logs and standard CloudWatch charges for publishing.
Under 'Pricing examples', the quote states an hourly fee for the Transit Gateway attachment.
The quote states IPsec VPN over Direct Connect encrypting traffic without public IP addresses or third-party VPN equipment.
The quote states it works over a Direct Connect transit VIF and uses a Direct Connect gateway and a transit gateway.
